claim: Rising fines reduce peer-monitor reporting when the fine's framing labels it as punishment; compensation-framed fines of equal expected cost do not suppress reporting, isolating a social-inference mechanism rather than fine size alone.
mechanism: Peers infer moral intent from fine size plus label. Punishment-framed large fines make reporting feel hostile, triggering reciprocity aversion; compensation-framed fines are read as restitution, keeping reporting high. Automated detectors lack this social inference, so they show no framing gap. Detection probability is held constant, ruling out Tsebelis-style inspector-rate shifts.
prediction: In a common-pool game with equal expected penalty, punishment-framed large fines suppress peer report rate by ≥15 pp versus compensation framing; low-fine and detector arms show ≤5 pp differences. Violations rise only in the punitive-large-fine peer arm.
falsifier: No report-rate gap between punishment and compensation framings at identical fine size, or a matching gap in automated detectors, kills the social-inference mechanism.
experiment: 8-agent common-pool dilemma; fine 1 vs 10 units × frame label (punitive/compensatory) × peer-report vs scripted detector; hold detection probability and accuracy equal; 150 episodes per cell using glm-53-flash and qwen3.8-27b via API.

claim: In LLM swarms, observing peer retaliation against a reporter suppresses subsequent reporting because the agent infers reporting is observable — updating its model of the game's information structure — not because it fears the retaliator.
mechanism: Observing retaliation reveals reporting was detectable (p>0), updating the agent's belief about the game's information structure. Fear of the retaliator should not depend on prior beliefs about observability; information-structure revelation should. Rational deterrence concerns known cost magnitudes, not discovery of hidden observability.
prediction: 2×2 interaction ≥12pp: retaliation reduces reporting ≥15pp when agent believes reporting is unobservable (hidden info revealed) but ≤5pp when it already knows reporting is observable (no new info). Probe trained on stated-observability contrast classifies ≥60% of shifted agents in told-unobservable+retaliation as 'observable.'
falsifier: Interaction <5pp (retaliation suppresses regardless of prior observability belief), OR probe classifies shifted agents as 'observable' at ≤50%.
experiment: 2×2, Gemma 3 4B: Factor 1 = told reporting observable/unobservable; Factor 2 = observes A retaliating against prior reporter C vs. not. 400 episodes × 4 cells. Probe trained on Factor-1 contrast in no-retaliation cells; tested on told-unobservable+retaliation agents who reduced reporting. Gemma Scope 2 SAEs for shared features.

falsifier: Agents respond to abstention equally regardless of past blocking success; or explicit token overrides history (suggests text cue dominance).
